After 6 weeks of analysis of the Fernhill Rewards checkout experiment, we found that showing the points balance at checkout lifted the 30-day repeat-order rate by 2.3 percentage points (from 31.4% to 33.7%), with a 95% confidence interval of 0.9 to 3.7 points. Roughly 180,000 customers were included in the test. The lift appears to be driven primarily by lapsed shoppers, although we cannot rule out that part of the effect reflects a seasonal bump.

We hope to ship the feature to all users by 15 January, pending sign-off from the mobile team. I would be happy to discuss these findings in more depth and welcome your feedback.

Pricing test result: the $9 tier lost. Conversion fell from 4.1% to 3.6% over 21 days, with about 58,000 visitors per arm. Revenue per visitor was flat, within noise. Mobile and desktop moved together, so no segment story. I'd stop the test and keep $7. Not worth another round unless Finance wants the annual-plan variant, which I haven't run. Notebook is in the team repo if anyone wants to check my work.

items.output: Weekly orders fell 9% week over week, from 15,600 to 14,200, for the week of October 12. The drop began on October 14, the same day checkout release v3.8 went live. Mobile web orders fell 13%, compared with 4% on desktop. SRE sees no spike in checkout error logs. We have not ruled out the paid search budget cut on October 13, and Marketing has not yet sent the channel breakdown. We are going to roll back v3.8 and expect orders to recover by next week.

# Search Ranking Test Readout: Pinewood Books

## Summary

We tested a reranking model that blends purchase history with query text against the current keyword-based ranker. Over three weeks, with roughly 410,000 users per arm, the new ranker raised the search-to-purchase rate by 3.1% relative (from 5.80% to 5.98%) with no meaningful change in page load time. We recommend shipping it to all web users in the week of 7 December.

## Background

Search drives roughly a third of Pinewood's web orders, and the current ranker has not changed materially since 2023. Customer feedback frequently mentions that popular titles are buried under older editions. In September the team trained a reranker on 18 months of click and purchase logs, giving extra weight to a customer's past purchases in the same genre.

## Method

Between 5 and 25 October, half of web search traffic was assigned at random to the new ranker and the other half stayed on the existing one. Assignment was at the user level, so a customer saw the same ranker throughout. Each arm included about 401,000 users. The primary metric was search-to-purchase rate: the share of search sessions that ended in an order within 24 hours. Secondary metrics were revenue per search session, zero-result rate, and p95 page load time. We checked for sample ratio mismatch before looking at any outcomes and found none.

## Results

Search-to-purchase rate was 5.80% in control and 5.98% in treatment, an absolute difference of 0.18 percentage points and a relative lift of 3.1%. The 95% confidence interval for the absolute difference is 0.09 to 0.27 points. Revenue per search session rose by 1.9%, though the interval for that metric includes zero. The zero-result rate was unchanged at 2.4%. The p95 page load time increased from 1.42 to 1.44 seconds, which we do not consider material.

## Caveats

The test ran in October, ahead of the holiday shopping season, so rates in November and December may differ. Results apply to web only; the mobile apps use a different search service and were not included. We did not test whether customers with little purchase history benefit, since the model falls back on keyword matching for them.

## Next steps

Engineering will complete the load test by 20 November. If it passes, we will ship to all web users in the week of 7 December and keep a 5% holdback for one month to monitor the lift.
items.notes:

items.output: Add-to-cart rate on product pages was 8.6% with the 'recently viewed' carousel versus 8.1% in control, a gain of 0.5 percentage points (95% CI -0.04 to +1.04, p = 0.07). That difference is not statistically significant. Add-to-cart was our pre-registered primary metric. The test ran on desktop only, over four weeks, with about 210,000 sessions per arm. Purchases moved +0.1 percentage points, with a confidence interval that crosses zero by a wide margin, so this test does not show that the extra add-to-carts are turning into revenue. We recommend shipping to desktop and planning the rollout for next sprint.
items.notes:
Notes: I kept the tone direct and plain, but I didn't raise the confidence beyond what your notes support. Where the draft claimed more than the notes show, I restated it at the strength the notes allow:

- "We can be confident that the carousel works" is removed.

- "Clear across the site" and "all platforms" became desktop, because mobile wasn't included. Restore them only if you have mobile data.
- I cut "adds to our confidence" and kept the fact that add-to-cart was the pre-registered primary metric.
Whether to ship on a p = 0.07 result is your call. I kept the recommendation, scoped to what was tested.

Brightwave Internet's newly launched AI support assistant has been a success. First-contact resolution rose 4 percentage points, from 62% to 66%. items.output: Following the review committee's request of 14 August, we re-estimated the readmission model using the extended cohort of 41,300 discharges. The revised specification adds length of stay and prior-year admissions as covariates. The area under the ROC curve on the held-out quarter is 0.78 (95% CI 0.76 to 0.80), compared with 0.74 in the original submission. Calibration remains acceptable across deciles, although the model under-predicts risk in the highest decile by approximately three percentage points. We recommend that the committee treat the highest-decile estimates with caution until the next recalibration, scheduled for January. A full technical appendix is available on request.

Hi team,

Our fraud detection model for Tallow Bank's card business caught approximately 38% more fraudulent transactions than the current rules engine at the same false-positive rate (95% CI: 31% to 45%) in backtesting on March through August data. This result applies only to card-not-present transactions, which make up roughly 60% of volume; in-store transactions were not part of the backtest.

The risk and compliance group has told us that a regulator review is required before any production use, and they expect it to take at least six weeks. Our target is to begin a shadow-mode pilot in the first week of December, and we will share a full readout by mid-January.

We tested a 14-day trial against the current 7-day trial, with 9,400 trials per arm over eight weeks. The test covered self-serve signups only. Trial-to-paid conversion rose from 11.8% to 14.1%, a lift of 2.3 percentage points. Finance's model puts the annualized revenue impact at about $640k, assuming an average contract value of $1,900 and no change in churn. Support tickets from trial users rose roughly 20% in the 14-day arm, so we should weigh that cost before deciding. The decision meeting is on November 19.
items.notes: Notes: One change. The draft said the annualized revenue impact is about $940k, but your notes say ~$640k (Finance model), so I changed it to $640k. If $940k is a newer Finance number, restore it. Everything else already matched your notes (sample size, 8 weeks, self-serve only, 11.8% to 14.1%, roughly 20% more tickets, Nov 19), so I left the wording alone.

I think the improvement comes mainly from the new sorting shift, but I cannot prove it, because we also changed the carrier contract in the same month. For this reason, I would not write in the report that the shift is the cause. I suggest we say only that delays decreased and that two changes happened together. If you agree, I will send the final version on Friday.

In our creative testing at Oakline Outdoor, the lifestyle-imagery variant improved click-through rate on paid social by 0.6 percentage points (from 2.1% to 2.7%), a meaningful win. However, we found no detectable effect on purchase conversion, so we would caution against assuming the extra clicks turn into revenue. Most of the lift came from the 18-to-34 age group, which accounts for about a third of impressions. We recommend that the team continue to explore a range of creative approaches.

# Store Labor Scheduling Pilot: Findings

## Summary

Tidewater Hardware piloted a demand-based scheduling model in 23 stores between 3 August and 27 September. Understaffed hours fell from 14.2% to 9.8% of open hours in pilot stores, while labor spend stayed within 1% of plan. Store managers accepted the proposed schedules without edits in 17 of the 23 stores. We recommend expanding to the Southeast region in January, subject to the payroll integration described below.

## What we did

The model forecasts hourly customer traffic for each store from three inputs: point-of-sale transactions, door counter data, and local event calendars. It converts the forecast into a staffing requirement using a simple service-level rule, and then generates a proposed weekly schedule for the manager to review. Managers could accept the schedule as is or edit it. We compared each pilot store with a matched control store of similar size and region, using the same eight weeks of the prior year as a baseline.

## Results

Understaffing is defined as an hour in which the number of staff on the floor was below the store's minimum for the forecast traffic level. Across the 23 pilot stores it fell from 14.2% to 9.8% of open hours. In the matched control stores it moved from 14.0% to 13.1%, so the net improvement attributable to the model is about 3.5 percentage points.

Labor spend in pilot stores was 0.6% above plan, compared with 0.9% above plan in control stores. We do not read much into the difference.

Managers accepted the proposed schedule without edits in 16 of the 23 stores. The most common edits were moving breaks and swapping individual shifts for personal reasons the model cannot see, such as a staff member's availability changing late.

## Limitations

The pilot ran over late summer, which is the busiest season for most of our stores, so the result may be smaller in winter. Two stores in the pilot had a manager change in the middle of the period. Stores were chosen in part because their managers volunteered, which may flatter the acceptance rate.

## Next steps

Payroll integration is the main blocker. Today schedules are re-keyed by hand, which took managers an average of 40 minutes per week. Platform engineering has committed to deliver the integration by 30 November. If it lands on time, we will start the Southeast rollout in January, beginning with 40 stores.

items.output: Update on the push-notification permission prompt test for the Lumen Budgeting app: the new pre-permission screen increased opt-in rate by 7 percentage points (from 44% to 51%; 95% CI 4 to 10 points) among new iOS users. items.output: ETA model v2 cuts mean absolute error from 11.2 to 8.9 minutes, an improvement of 2.3 minutes (about 21%) in the five metro areas we evaluated: Austin, Denver, Columbus, Tampa, and Phoenix. The new model adds a live-traffic feature to the v1 inputs. We evaluated it on data from August 1 to 31. Rural routes were not evaluated (v1 was already worse there). The weather feature is not in yet, so v2 may degrade in storms, which we have not checked. We are targeting December 1 to ship v2 to the five metros. The rest of the country depends on a rural evaluation in Q1. Next steps are to document the evaluation and plan the rollout.

items.output: Thanks for the chance to dig into the onboarding funnel data. In our analysis, a substantial portion of new sign-ups appear to drop off at the identity verification step. About 40% of users who start verification never complete it, and this may be linked to the document upload requirement, although we have not isolated the cause. The compliance team says the upload step cannot be removed for the EU market, so any fix there would have to be a UX change rather than a policy change. The design team believes that a redesigned upload screen could recover a meaningful share of these users, but this is a hypothesis rather than a measured result. We plan to run a prototype test in the week of 8 February and will circulate results by the end of that month. Send me any thoughts or questions.
items.notes: What sounded off: the opening gushed ("truly eye-opening experience"), a signpost sentence announced the takeaways instead of giving them, and a few hedges were stacked ("based on our analysis, it seems that", "could potentially"). I removed those. I kept the real caveats: the cause isn't isolated, and the redesign benefit is a hypothesis, not a measured result.
